The ten-year adverse possession period

Arizona protects a person who has peaceable, adverse possession of land and is cultivating, using and enjoying it, but only after the owner has sat on the claim for ten years from when the cause of action accrued (section 12-526). An owner who wants the land back must file suit inside that window.

The claim has a ceiling: no more than 160 acres, improvements included, or the acreage actually enclosed if that is smaller. Where someone took possession under a recorded written memorandum of title (other than a deed) that fixes boundaries, the claim extends to the boundaries in that paper.

For a homeowner the takeaway is calm. Someone who walks into a vacant house does not hold title a week later. The ten-year rule targets long, open, uncontested use, and an owner who acts early keeps control.

Squatter or tenant

They differ in one basic way. A tenant has an agreement with the owner, while a squatter has none. That difference drives which court process the owner uses.

Arizona's forcible detainer law reaches beyond tenants. Under section 12-1173.01, a person who stays after written demand can be removed through a forcible detainer action filed with the clerk of the superior court when the property:

  • was sold through foreclosure of a mortgage, deed of trust or contract for conveyance,
  • was sold at a trustee's sale under a deed of trust,
  • was forfeited under a contract for conveyance,
  • was sold under an execution and title has been duly transferred, or
  • was sold by the owner and title has been duly transferred.

People holding a lease or another possessory right that outranks the interest sold are protected. These remedies sit beside other remedies and do not replace them.

How quickly the eviction case moves

Forcible detainer is meant to be fast. The complaint is made in writing and under oath to the superior court clerk or a justice of the peace. Then section 12-1175 requires the summons to issue by the next judicial day, with service at least two days before the return date.

Describe the premises well enough to identify them, and state the facts that entitle you to possession. State agencies and individual courts may not require one mandatory form for notices or pleadings, provided the document meets the content rules.

Next comes trial. When the plaintiff asks for a jury, section 12-1176 says the request must be granted, and trial happens within five judicial days of filing. Superior court juries have eight members and justice court juries have six. A defendant may request a jury if the plaintiff doesn't.

After the judge rules for the owner

A defendant found guilty of forcible detainer faces judgment for restitution of the premises and a writ of restitution. The court under section 12-1178 may add damages, attorney fees and costs, plus unpaid rent when a rental agreement is involved.

StageWhat happens
Judgment for plaintiffRestitution of the premises, damages, fees and costs, and a writ of restitution
Waiting periodNo writ issues until five calendar days after judgment
Motion to set asideDoes not stop the writ unless a judge finds good cause
Judgment for defendantDefendant gets damages, fees and costs, and a writ if the plaintiff took possession in the meantime
Staying after service of writCriminal trespass in the third degree under 13-1502 for a dwelling unit, mobile home space or RV space

A losing defendant must be given notice of that trespass rule by the court.

Is entering a vacant house a crime?

It may be. Criminal trespass in the first degree, defined in section 13-1504, includes knowingly entering or staying unlawfully in a residential structure or a fenced residential yard. The structure version is a class 6 felony, and the fenced-yard version is a class 1 misdemeanor.

The same law reaches someone who enters a residential yard and looks into the home in reckless disregard of the occupant's privacy, also a class 1 misdemeanor. Because this is a police matter, ask officers how they handle it, and ask an attorney whether a civil case should run alongside.

Never change locks, cut utilities or haul out belongings from an occupied home without legal advice. The court tools above exist so owners can reach a lawful result.

If you find someone inside

Stay calm and keep the sequence in order. Don't confront the person, and don't try to force them out yourself.

  1. Call the police and get a report number, since entering or staying in a residence unlawfully can be a crime.
  2. Photograph the property and write down dates, names and anything the person says about permission.
  3. Check whether the person claims a lease or other right. A tenant and a trespasser are handled differently.
  4. Serve a written demand to leave, then file the forcible detainer complaint if the person stays.
  5. Attend the trial, and once judgment is entered, wait out the five calendar days before the writ.

An attorney can tell you which step applies to your facts. Courts work quickly on these cases, so having your deed and photos ready saves days.

Protecting a vacant house

Attention is the best defense. With a ten-year period and the right to sue at any point before it ends, what matters is noticing trouble early and answering it.

  • Visit on a schedule and keep a dated log with photos.
  • Keep taxes, insurance and utilities current in the owner's or the estate's name.
  • Secure doors, windows and gates, and post clear no-trespassing signs.
  • Give neighbors a number to call if they see activity.
  • If someone is inside, get the police report number and ask an attorney about written demand and a forcible detainer complaint.

Vacant houses tend to be inherited homes, rentals after a tenant leaves, or properties in probate. Those are also the houses people ask us to buy. If managing a neglected or occupied house is wearing you down, selling as-is for cash is one way out.

Selling with a squatter inside

A sale can happen, but the occupant affects price, timing and how comfortable the title company feels. A cash buyer may accept an occupied property as-is, with the price reflecting that. Closing still depends on the title company confirming who can sign and what is recorded against the property.

Tell us the facts: how long the person has been there, whether anyone gave permission, whether you served a written demand, and whether a case has been filed. We buy houses across Arizona in any condition, and we'll explain what we can and can't do with those facts.

Before you call, gather the deed, any police report number, copies of notices you sent and photos of the property. Those papers let us and the title company move faster, and they help an attorney too.

Frequently asked questions

How many years of adverse possession are required in Arizona?

Ten years of peaceable, adverse possession, after which the owner can no longer sue. The claim is capped at 160 acres, or the enclosed acreage if smaller.

How fast is an Arizona forcible detainer trial?

Trial is set no more than five judicial days after the complaint is filed. The summons issues by the next judicial day and must be served at least two days before the return date.

How long until a writ of restitution is issued in Arizona?

Not before five calendar days after judgment. A motion to set aside the judgment won't delay the writ unless a judge finds good cause.

Is staying in a house after a writ of restitution a crime in Arizona?

Yes. A defendant served with the writ who stays in or returns to the dwelling without the owner's permission commits criminal trespass in the third degree under 13-1502.

Is unlawful entry into a residence a felony in Arizona?

Entering or remaining unlawfully in a residential structure is first-degree criminal trespass and a class 6 felony. In a fenced residential yard it is a class 1 misdemeanor.

Arizona Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Written disclosures a landlord owes

By the start of a tenancy, an Arizona landlord has to put two things in writing for the tenant: the name and address of the person who manages the premises, and the name and address of an owner or agent who can accept legal papers and notices. The landlord must also state in writing that the Arizona residential landlord and tenant act is posted on the Arizona Department of Housing website.

The information has to stay current and be provided again whenever the tenant asks. Any successor landlord, owner or manager takes on the same duty, which matters when a house changes hands. A landlord who skips these steps becomes an agent of every landlord for service of process and for receiving notices and demands.

With a written lease, the landlord hands over a signed copy, the tenant returns one fully signed copy, and every blank space gets filled in. Whichever side fails to do this is materially out of compliance.

When rent is due and what an open-ended tenancy means

Unless the parties agreed otherwise, rent is payable at the dwelling at the start of the period, with no demand or notice needed. Monthly rent falls due at the start of each month, and a partial month is prorated evenly by the day.

With no lease at all, the tenant owes the fair rental value of the unit. When a lease sets no definite term, the tenancy runs month to month, except that a roomer paying weekly rent has a week-to-week tenancy.

These defaults come up when someone inherits or buys a house with a tenant who never signed anything. That tenant still has statutory rights, so find out what the real arrangement is before closing.

Lease clauses Arizona does not allow

A rental agreement can't make a tenant give up the rights and remedies the act provides, and a clause that tries is unenforceable. The statute names five prohibited promises:

  • Waiving rights or remedies under the landlord tenant chapter.
  • Paying the landlord's attorney fees, although a written lease may let the prevailing party in court recover fees.
  • Excusing the landlord from liability, or agreeing to indemnify the landlord for it.
  • Giving up the right to call police or emergency help.
  • Paying a penalty because the tenant, or anyone else, called for emergency help.

A landlord who knowingly uses a lease with such terms can owe the tenant actual damages plus up to two months of periodic rent. If you're a landlord and a seller, have an attorney read an older lease before you give it to a buyer, because a bad clause can create exposure.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Arizona house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Ending a tenancy for nonpayment or breach

How long a tenant gets depends on the problem. For unpaid rent, the landlord gives written notice and the tenant has five days to pay before a special detainer action can be filed. Most other material breaches come with ten days to fix. A serious health or safety breach by the tenant gets five days. A material and irreparable breach, such as violence, certain drug activity or serious property damage, allows an immediate termination notice.

Lying on the rental application about occupants, pets, income or prior evictions is also a breach. Falsifying criminal history or prior evictions can't be cured.

ProblemTime the tenant has
Unpaid rentFive days after written notice
Material breach of the leaseTen days to cure
Breach affecting health and safetyFive days to cure
Material and irreparable breachImmediate termination notice

A notice sent by certified mail counts as received on the day it's actually delivered or five days after mailing, whichever is first.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying?

Sometimes. Before a special detainer action is filed, the lease is reinstated when the tenant pays all past due rent plus a reasonable late fee set out in the written lease. After filing, reinstatement also takes attorney fees and court costs. Once the landlord has a judgment, reinstating is up to the landlord.

Tenants can't hold back rent for reasons the act doesn't authorize. One authorized route is self-help for minor defects. If the landlord fails to meet habitability duties and the repair costs less than $300 or half of one month's rent, whichever is more, the tenant may give written notice and wait ten days. After that, a contractor with a license can do the work, and the tenant deducts the cost from rent after giving the landlord an itemized statement and a lien waiver. That route is closed when the tenant or a guest caused the damage.

How fast a special detainer case moves

The process is quick by design. A summons is issued the day the complaint is filed, and the return date falls no fewer than three and no more than six days after the summons date. Service must happen at least two days before the return day.

If personal service is tried and fails, the landlord can finish service by posting a copy on the front entrance within one day and mailing a copy by certified mail the same day. The tenant is treated as served three days after mailing. For good cause backed by an affidavit, a trial can be postponed by up to three days in justice court or five days in superior court.

When the landlord wins, the court enters judgment for possession, stated late charges, costs, and at the landlord's option the unpaid rent, then issues a writ of restitution. For a material and irreparable breach, trial is set within three days of filing, and restitution is ordered at least twelve and no more than twenty four hours after a finding.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Arizona houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

If a tenant dies or can't be reached

A landlord may ask the tenant to name a person who can enter the unit to retrieve belongings and any pet if the tenant dies or becomes incapacitated. If the landlord can't reach that person, or the person doesn't respond within one day for an animal or ten days for other property after written contact, the landlord may dispose of the property under the abandoned property statute.

The named person must show government photo identification. They have twenty days after first written contact, or after the last paid rent date if later, to remove items and return the keys. Once the landlord lets the person in, the landlord has no further liability for those items. These personal property rules apply when periodic rent has gone unpaid for at least five days.

Before you sell a rented Arizona house

Know exactly what the lease and the statute require before a buyer asks. Work through this list:

  • Confirm the written disclosure of manager and owner contact details was given and is current.
  • Gather the signed lease, any addenda, and records of rent paid and late fees charged.
  • Read the lease for prohibited clauses and fix the paperwork if needed.
  • Check whether the tenancy is month to month, since that sets the notice needed to end it.
  • Document open repair requests, because unresolved habitability problems give the tenant remedies.

A buyer who takes the house as-is usually steps into the landlord's position, deposit duties included, so share the lease file early. If you're in a dispute with a tenant, treat the notice rules as firm and talk to an attorney before serving anything. The statute spells out how notices must be delivered and what they must say.

Frequently asked questions

How many days does a tenant have to pay rent after notice in Arizona?

Five days. If the tenant doesn't pay within five days of the landlord's written notice of nonpayment, the landlord may file a special detainer action.

How long does a landlord wait for a tenant to fix a lease breach?

Ten days for most material breaches, and five days when the breach affects health and safety. A material and irreparable breach can lead to immediate termination notice.

Can an Arizona lease make a tenant pay the landlord's attorney fees?

Not as a one-sided term. A written lease may let the prevailing party recover fees, but a clause making only the tenant pay the landlord's fees is prohibited and unenforceable.

Is a notice sent by certified mail effective right away?

No. It counts as received the day it actually arrives or five days after mailing, whichever happens first.

What is a special detainer action?

It's the court case a landlord files to recover possession of a rental for nonpayment or breach. The summons issues the day of filing and the return date is set three to six days later.

Arizona Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Arizona Eviction Notice Rules sale

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Arizona?

Which notice fits which problem?

Choosing the right Arizona notice starts with the reason: rent not paid, a lease violation, a health and safety violation, a breach that can't be repaired, or a periodic tenancy that's simply ending. The statute assigns a different count of days to each, and a landlord who grabs the wrong one risks losing the case.

Reason for the noticeHow long the tenant has
Unpaid rent5 days after written notice
Material lease breachEnds no sooner than 10 days after receipt if not fixed in 10 days
Health and safety breach under 33-1341Ends no sooner than 5 days after receipt if not fixed in 5 days
Material and irreparable breachImmediate termination notice
Month-to-month tenancy30 days before the rental date
Week-to-week tenancy10 days before the termination date

Inside A.R.S. 33-1368 the word days is defined as calendar days, which means Saturdays and Sundays are counted. The two periodic tenancy rules come from A.R.S. 33-1375.

What a five-day nonpayment notice must say

Three things belong in it. It's written, it states that rent hasn't been paid, and it warns that the landlord means to terminate the rental agreement unless the rent arrives within five days. Subsection 33-1368(B) supplies that language.

Timing matters too. A landlord has to wait until after the last day of the notice before filing. The court must dismiss the case if the tenant didn't get a proper termination notice with a chance to pay the rent and late fees, or if the notice wasn't served correctly.

Arizona doesn't dictate a form. Under A.R.S. 12-1175(D), no state agency or individual court may adopt or enforce a rule that makes a mandatory or technical form necessary for notices or pleadings in these cases, provided the notice meets the statutory content requirements.

How a notice is delivered and when it counts as received

Delivery rules are in A.R.S. 33-1313. A notice reaches the tenant when someone hands it over, or when it's mailed by registered or certified mail to the address the tenant designated, or to the last known residence when none was designated.

Mail adds a wrinkle. The tenant is considered to have received it on the date it truly arrives or five days after it was mailed, whichever is earlier. Since the 5-day and 10-day periods in 33-1368 run from receipt, a mailed notice lengthens the schedule.

For a clean record, many landlords hand-deliver and keep proof of it, or send certified mail and keep the receipt.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Arizona house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Ten-day and five-day lease breach notices

These notices give the tenant a chance to fix the problem, and if it's fixed in time the lease continues. The 10-day notice must describe the acts and omissions that make up the breach and state that the agreement ends on a date at least ten days after receipt if the breach isn't remedied within ten days.

A few details from the statute:

  • Material falsification on the rental application can be a breach, for example untrue information about occupants, pets, income or employment.
  • Falsification about criminal records, prior evictions or current criminal activity can't be cured under that section.
  • A five-day health and safety notice must be cured within five days. If repair or payment of damages fixes the breach before the date in the notice, the agreement doesn't end.
  • If the same or a similar health and safety problem returns during the lease after a cure, the landlord may file a special detainer action ten days after delivering written notice of the second noncompliance.

When a landlord can terminate immediately

Immediate termination is reserved for a breach that is both material and irreparable and that happens on the premises. The statute gives examples and says the list isn't exhaustive:

  • Illegal discharge of a weapon
  • Homicide, prostitution, or criminal street gang activity
  • Unlawful manufacturing, selling, using or storing of a controlled substance
  • Threatening or intimidating, or assault
  • Acts found to be a nuisance, or breaches that endanger the health, safety and welfare of the landlord, agent or another tenant, or involve imminent or actual serious property damage

After filing under A.R.S. 33-1377, the trial date and return date must be set no later than the third day after filing. If the court finds the breach occurred by a preponderance of the evidence, it must order restitution not less than 12 nor more than 24 hours later.

Ending a month-to-month tenancy before a sale

To close out a month-to-month tenancy, someone gives written notice at least 30 days ahead of the periodic rental date stated in it, and either the landlord or the tenant can do that. A week-to-week tenancy needs the written notice at least ten days before it ends.

A tenant who remains after the term ends, or after termination, without the landlord's consent exposes themselves to a possession suit. If the holdover is willful and not in good faith, the landlord may also collect up to two months of periodic rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is larger.

Consent in writing from the landlord changes the analysis, so any deal that lets a tenant stay past a sale belongs on paper.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Arizona houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How accepting rent can weaken a notice

Taking rent after a default can waive the right to terminate for that breach. A.R.S. 33-1371 provides that, apart from listed exceptions, accepting rent or any part of it while aware of a default waives the right to terminate for that breach.

A landlord needn't accept partial payment. One who does keeps the right to proceed only if the tenant agrees to the terms in a contemporaneous writing that includes a date when the balance is due. A housing assistance payment is treated differently: accepting it isn't accepting a partial payment and doesn't waive termination.

Showing the house to buyers

Before entering, a landlord owes the tenant at least two days' notice and must pick reasonable times. Emergencies, and situations where notice can't practically be given, are exceptions. The rule is A.R.S. 33-1343.

That statute also says the tenant can't unreasonably refuse consent when the landlord wants to show the unit to prospective or actual purchasers. In return, access can't be misused to harass the tenant, and the landlord has no other way in except a court order, the abandonment rules, or surrender of the premises.

Planning to sell a rented house? Build your showing schedule around the two-day minimum and keep a written log of every notice you give.

When retaliation bars a notice

Raising rent, reducing services or threatening to sue for possession in response to a tenant's complaint is retaliation, and it's off limits. A.R.S. 33-1381 covers complaints to a housing or building code agency about a health and safety violation, complaints made to the landlord under 33-1324, and joining a tenants' union.

Six months is the line that matters. If the tenant complained within six months before the landlord acted, the law presumes retaliation. The landlord keeps the right to sue when rent is in default, or when the code violation came mostly from the tenant's own lack of reasonable care.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How many days is an eviction notice in Arizona?

It depends on the reason: five days for unpaid rent after written notice, ten days for a curable lease breach, five days for a health and safety breach, and an immediate notice for a material and irreparable breach. A month-to-month tenancy needs 30 days.

Do weekends count toward the five-day notice?

Yes. For A.R.S. 33-1368, days means calendar days.

Can a landlord evict without a written notice?

For nonpayment and lease breaches the statute calls for written notice. The case must be dismissed if the tenant wasn't given a proper notice and a chance to pay.

Does a landlord have to use a particular form?

No. A.R.S. 12-1175(D) bars courts and state agencies from requiring a mandatory or technical form, as long as the notice meets the statutory content requirements.

Can a landlord show the house to buyers while it is tenant-occupied?

Yes, with at least two days' notice at reasonable times, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent. Emergencies and impracticable situations are excepted.
